title: The Most Dangerous Moment in Any Decision Is the Moment You Feel Sure (leadwithkelly.substack.com), September 1, 2026
author: Kelly McGinnis
source: Lead with Kelly McGinnis (leadwithkelly.substack.com), Lead with Kelly McGinnis
summary: Kelly McGinnis recounts being served a lawsuit after poaching a top mechanical engineering team for a startup, and uses the story to unpack how certainty about one part of a decision can quietly justify ignoring everything else that is uncertain or visibly wrong. She had correctly judged the engineers as extraordinary talent, but that correctness masked two problems she could see clearly and chose to move past anyway: a deep cultural contempt between the company's software and mechanical engineering camps, and an unproven market that never converted interest into contracts. The team's talent was never in question; the culture clash she had watched happen in the room was what actually sank the bet, and the market simply never showed up. McGinnis draws the lesson that the moment a decision 'feels sure' is precisely the moment to interrogate what that certainty is letting you skip checking, since confidence about one measurable fact easily bleeds into false confidence about unmeasurable risks. The essay is a personal failure narrative aimed at leaders making high-stakes people and strategy decisions.
points: Uses a personal story -- being sued after hiring away a mechanical engineering team -- to illustrate how being right about one thing (the talent) can obscure being wrong about everything else (culture, market, strategy).
Distinguishes between 'a gap I could fix' and 'an unknown I could not know,' arguing that real decisions are made in that fog rather than after it clears.
Describes watching two internal 'tribes' -- software engineers and mechanical engineers -- hold mutual contempt before the hire was ever made, and admits the warning signs were never hidden.
Names the core failure mode: certainty about the one thing you can measure quietly becomes false certainty about the things you cannot measure.
Reframes a 'clean, confident hum' in decision-making as a warning sign rather than a green light, prescribing a habit of interrogating exactly the part of a decision that feels most certain.
quotes: A man knocked on my door in San Francisco and handed me legal papers. I was being sued for the people I had just hired. The ink on their offers was barely dry.

There was a problem I could see clearly. The company was full of brilliant software people and almost no one who understood the machines. You cannot predict when a machine will fail if no one in the building knows how it works.
So I was about to hand the best mechanical engineers in the world to a company that believed mechanical engineers were a thing of the past. Two tribes. Each was certain the other was beneath them.

The people were everything I said they were. It was beside the point. The outcome was never going to be decided by talent. It was going to be decided by a culture I had watched reject the idea of them before they ever arrived.
That is the trap. Certainty about the one thing you can measure becomes certainty about the things you cannot. Will the market show? Will the cultures merge? Can I hold this together on will alone?
Now, when a decision gives off that clean, confident hum, the part that says, "At least this choice I know for sure," I have learned to treat it as the warning, not the green light.
